contentBlocks.text: You've learned how character comes through dialogue. Today: a powerful tool playwrights use called dramatic irony!

Dramatic irony happens when the audience knows something important that one or more characters on stage do not — this creates tension, because the audience is waiting to see how the character will react when they finally find out. Read this short scene: (The audience has just seen TOMAS hide a surprise party invitation in his bag.) MAYA: Why do you keep checking your bag? TOMAS: No reason. Just making sure I have everything. Explain why this moment is an example of dramatic irony, and what tension it creates for the audience.
You just learned how dramatic irony creates tension! Tomorrow we'll put dialogue, character, and irony together in one scene.

objectives: Define dramatic irony as the audience knowing something a character doesn't
Identify dramatic irony in the TOMAS/MAYA scene and explain the tension it creates
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's dialogue and character work briefly.
2. Introduce dramatic irony and read the TOMAS/MAYA scene together.
3. Have the child explain why it's dramatic irony and what tension it creates.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's combined-analysis lesson.
differentiationTips: Struggling: point out explicitly that the audience saw something MAYA didn't (the hidden invitation) before asking the child to explain why that matters
Ready for more: ask the child to think of a movie or show they've seen that used dramatic irony, and briefly describe the scene
Dramatic irony is a genuinely powerful, widely-used technique worth spending real time on — it appears constantly in the plays and shows students already know
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is dramatic irony because the audience already knows TOMAS is hiding a surprise party invitation, but MAYA doesn't — this creates tension because the audience is watching MAYA get suspicious and waiting to see whether TOMAS's secret will be revealed or whether the surprise will succeed.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses Common Core Grade 9-10 RL.9-10.4/RL.9-10.5: analyzing an author's choices concerning structure and how specific dramatic techniques create meaning and tension.
